newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Japan group returns to disputed isles -Taiwan TV.
newsitem.headline: Japan group returns to disputed isles -Taiwan TV.

text.p: Japanese rightists returned on Monday to the disputed Diaoyu islands to reassert a claim that has embroiled Japan, Taiwan and China in a sovereignty dispute, Taiwan Television reported.
The state-run channel aired videotape shot from a plane showing a half-dozen men repairing the makeshift lighthouse first built in July by the right-wing Japan Youth Federation.
Taiwan Television said the same group had returned to the uninhabited island to repair damage inflicted by a typhoon in August, but did not say how it identified them from the air.
In Tokyo, a spokesman for the rightist group would not confirm media reports that its members were involved.

Tokyo has effectively supported the group's moves to bolster Japan's claim to the islands, mobilising coast guard ships to repel private Taiwan vessels that have tried to reach the Diaoyus in recent days.
"We have heard that the Taiwan media reported this, but have not verified the report," said an official at the Maritime Safety Agency.
Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government said on Monday it could defend its claim to the islands and would not cooperate with rival claimant China to solve the dispute with Japan.

"The government of the Republic of China has the ability to resolve the dispute, and does not need to cooperate with outside forces, including the mainland, and further complicate the matter," Foreign Minister John Chang said on state television.
China and Taiwan have been political rivals since a civil war split them in 1949, and are believed to be uncomfortable with the rare confluence of their interests.
"Our government has responsilibity to face and solve the problem of seeking sovereignty over the Diaoyu islands and negotiating with Japan over fishing rights," Chang said.
Taiwan would send officials to Japan "as soon as possible" to discuss related issues, Chang said.
Taiwan fishermen say Japan's exercising of claims to the Diaoyu chain has squeezed them out of bountiful fishing waters.
The Diaoyus, known as the Senkakus in Japanese, lie in the East China Sea west of Japan's Okinawa island, northeast of Taiwan and east of China's southeastern Fujian coast.
Japan's moves have angered Chinese in Hong Kong and mainland China as well as in Taiwan, uniting the three regions despite their own political differences.
Angry Taiwan residents on Sunday formed an alliance to protect the Diaoyus from Japan and threatened to organise mass protests against what they called Tokyo's invasion.
A poll published on Monday showed that 69 percent of 982 Taiwanese interviewed by the mass circulation United Daily News said they wanted Taipei to send vessels to protect the islands.
Dissatisfaction runs strong, with 58 percent saying the government had taken too soft a stance toward Japan.
Only 38 percent said they would support military actions taken by communist China to protect the islands, while 45 percent said they would not support such moves.

China angrily denounced the construction of the lighthouse in July but recently has toned down its rhetoric, prompting some analysts to speculate that Beijing fears losing huge Japanese investments in its economy.
Taiwan's foreign ministry has protested to Japan over the Diaoyu issue, urging Tokyo to use restraint.
China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries. Tokyo's claim dates to 1895 when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories.
